extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and scholars of British television and political satire
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the features, techniques and production choices that make the British sitcom Yes Minister an effective piece of political satire — useful for analyzing or producing political-satire television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirise politics and government, not a specific party
rubrics_metrics.description: The series 'intended to satirise politics and government in general, rather than any specific party' and 'the terms "Labour" and "Conservative" are scrupulously avoided throughout the series.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep satire broadly targeted at institutions and behaviours rather than party labels; use neutral signifiers (the show used a white rosette) and avoid explicit partisan references so humour remains universal and not alienating to half the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour derives from antagonism between ministers and the civil service
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Much of the show's humour thus derives from the antagonism between Cabinet ministers (who believe they are in charge) and the members of the British Civil Service (who believe they really run the country).’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center episodes on the conflict of interests and motives between political actors and bureaucrats. Comedy should expose how public-spirited rhetoric collides with institutional self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use private, behind-closed-doors settings
rubrics_metrics.description: The writers placed most scenes in private locations (offices, exclusive members' clubs) because 'government does not take place in the House of Commons... Government happens in private.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage political action in intimate, private settings where backstage manoeuvring and subtle manipulation can be shown; minimise parliamentary/public spectacle scenes unless the point is to contrast them with private reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-defined archetypal character roles and dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Core trio: the Minister (Jim Hacker) — publicity-seeking, idealistic then increasingly sly; the Permanent Secretary (Sir Humphrey) — committed to the status quo, master of obfuscation and manipulation; the Principal Private Secretary (Bernard) — split loyalties, pedant and mediator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make character traits consistent and complementary so dramatic conflict and comic payoff arise naturally. Each role has a functional purpose in the satire (political idealism vs. bureaucratic preservation vs. intermediary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obfuscation, circumlocution and long-winded jargon as a comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir Humphrey is described as 'a master of obfuscation and manipulation, baffling his opponents with long-winded technical jargon and circumlocutions' and often uses committees and red tape to smother proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inflated, vague or pseudo-technical language to comedic effect; show how verbosity conceals motive or frustrates action. Tactics include inventing committees, legalistic wording, acronyms, and proceduralism.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Big speeches’ and rhetorical grandstanding for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'big speeches' (including Churchillian-style orations) are recurring comedic set-pieces — both as performance moments and as devices that reveal character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write memorable, rhetorically ornate speeches that can be undercut by context or show speaker's self-importance; rehearse and stage them as highlights of episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode structure: proposal → stalling tactics → resolution (often ironic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical episode centres on Hacker's proposing a reform and Sir Humphrey's blocking of all Hacker's approaches; episodes revolve around proposals backed by Hacker but frustrated by Appleby or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build plots around a clear policy proposal or initiative, introduce bureaucratic countermeasures (five-step stalling, white papers, committees, staffing maneuvers), and resolve with either a hollow victory, ironic compromise, or exposed failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bernard's 'walk the tightrope' — balancing loyalties via elaborate verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernard must 'walk the tightrope' between minister and civil service, 'resorting to elaborate verbosity... so that he can avoid the appearance of being disloyal to one, in favour of the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an intermediary character who signals both sides' intentions and provides comic commentary; their evasive or pedantic language can be a steady source of humour and plot movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground plots in real-life inspiration and insider detail for authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers drew on insiders, published material and real events; 'after inventing this absurdity, we discovered there were six such hospitals... exactly as we had described them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research real bureaucratic practices, leaks and anecdotes. Authentic, plausible details often produce funnier and more resonant satire than pure invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overt partisanship by centring the protagonist on the political spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: The writers 'placed Hacker at the centre of the political spectrum' so the target is governmental process rather than a particular ideology or party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position protagonists so their motives are recognisable across audiences; this neutrality lets satire critique systems and behaviours rather than alienating viewers with partisan attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-level comic techniques: mixed metaphors, pedantry and lexical play
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour uses mixed metaphors, pedantry (Bernard pointing out impossibilities), Latin/Greek references, and verbal one-upmanship to create comic tension and reveal character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ precise comic language devices: pedantic corrections, deliberately malformed metaphors, learned references used to confuse, and pointed one-liners to puncture pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal and performance emphasis for lengthy dialogue exchanges
rubrics_metrics.description: Producer Sydney Lotterby said he always tried to give the actors extra time to rehearse as their scenes invariably featured lengthy dialogue exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate rehearsal time and directorial attention to verbal exchanges; timing and delivery are crucial for long verbal comic scenes to land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening titles and theme music to establish tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Gerald Scarfe's caricature opening titles and Ronnie Hazlehurst's Westminster-Quarters–inspired theme music set the satirical, Whitehall-linked tone of the series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual and musical motifs (caricature, state chimes, institutional graphic elements) to prime the audience for the show's satirical register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurring supporting characters to expand satirical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A cast of recurring characters (advisors, press secretaries, permanent secretaries, Chief Whips, etc.) allow exploration of many bureaucratic angles and sustain continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce recurring archetypal figures who can be recycled into different plotlines to illuminate various institutional practices and provide running jokes or continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department as a versatile vehicle to explore varied political themes
rubrics_metrics.description: The fictional Department of Administrative Affairs serves to explore foreign policy, education, the environment, health, defence, Europe, trade, local government, infrastructure and national security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a bureaucratic setting with jurisdictional breadth so writers can plausibly attach diverse issues to the central location, enabling varied episodic themes while keeping consistent locale and cast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire that trains the audience to 'unpick verbal tricks' of politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Armando Iannucci suggested the show 'taught us how to unpick the verbal tricks that politicians think they can get away with in front of the cameras.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft scenes that explicitly reveal rhetorical evasions and procedural smokescreens so the audience learns to spot rather than simply laugh at political obfuscation; this increases satirical bite and cultural impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy from character contradictions and sudden switches of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: All characters are able to 'switch to a completely opposite opinion in seconds when convenient.' This fluidity is a recurrent source of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit opportunistic reversals and hypocrisy as comic tools: rapid U-turns, pragmatic rationalisations, and self-serving consistency lapses reveal institutional absurdities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend comedic intent with an explanatory/ideological subtext (public choice economics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jay noted that public choice economics — the idea that government decisions are often conflicts of private interest — 'was at the root of almost every episode.' Some critics saw ideological content alongside comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave an explanatory subtext (e.g., incentives, institutional self-interest) beneath jokes so satire has explanatory power; be aware this can be read as ideological framing and may attract critique.
